item.title: Michigan fans called out on social media for rushing field after Wolverines steal win over Western Michigan
item.description: Michigan fans stormed the field after Bryce Underwood's Hail Mary saved a 13-12 win over Western Michigan, sparking college football debate.
item.content:encoded:
Emotions are what make college football great, but there is a fine line between showing raw emotions and letting emotions get the best of you. The latter happened in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on Saturday night.

The Michigan Wolverines were beaten – and some would say literally – by Western Michigan on Saturday before one of the more unbelievable scenes in the sport's history unfolded.

After Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood sailed his Hail Mary attempt out of the back of the endzone and the clock hit triple zeros, the officials reviewed the play and elected to put one second back on the clock. The video review seen on the NBC broadcast left no doubt that time had expired on the clocks available to the network, but a second was added, and the rest is history.

CLOCK CONTROVERSY ALLOWS MICHIGAN WOLVERINES TO AVOID MASSIVE UPSET AGAINST WESTERN MICHIGAN

Underwood's second Hail Mary attempt was perfect as he lobbed a pass to the goal line for 6-foot-4 receiver JJ Buchanan to go up and get it, and get it he did.

With Michigan stealing a 13-12 win over the Broncos in dramatic fashion, the fans who stuck around in The Big House stormed the field to celebrate. While the Wolverines have gone through a significant amount of change in leadership and coaching in recent months, it's still the same Michigan that is just three years removed from winning a national title, and its fans rushing the field after beating a MAC team was quite the scene.

The Wolverines were four-touchdown favorites heading into Saturday's contest against the Broncos.

College football fans were quick to call out the celebrations that broke out on the field in Ann Arbor.

While the last-second drama added some much-needed fuel to a relatively lackluster Week 1 of college football, the addition of time back on the clock, coupled with a fanbase of a blue-blood program storming the field after scoring 13 points against a MAC, turned into the headline as opposed to the final play itself.

Michigan welcomes Oklahoma to town in Week 2. It goes without saying that the Wolverines will need to improve in a hurry if they want to compete against the Top 10 Sooners.

item.title: Texas deputy screams and runs after 'dead' deer springs to feet in viral encounter
item.description: The viral video has racked up over 10 million views as an East Texas sheriff's deputy discovers a motionless doe is very much alive during a night shift, a sheriff said.
item.content:encoded:
An East Texas sheriff’s deputy got the scare of his life when a deer he thought was dead suddenly sprang to its feet, sending the startled lawman screaming back toward his cruiser in a moment caught on camera that quickly went viral online.

The wild encounter was captured on the deputy’s dashcam and shared on Facebook by Trinity County Sheriff Woody Wallace, who joked that sometimes things can "scare the heck out of a person."

Wallace had some fun with the incident, encouraging social media users to "[w]atch when he encounters what he thinks is a dead deer until it comes back to life!"

The video opens with the deputy approaching what appears to be a motionless doe lying along the side of the road.

BIG SKY, MONTANA WILDLIFE ENCOUNTER CAUGHT ON VIDEO AS MOOSE CHARGES TOWARD WOMAN AND HER DOGS

As the deputy gets closer to examine the animal, the deer suddenly springs to life.

The startled deputy lets out a scream and races back toward his patrol vehicle.

"Okay, we’re good," the deputy says with a laugh after recovering from the surprise.

The deer is last seen sitting up on the side of the road before the video ends.

LATE-NIGHT BULL RUN ENDS WITH A LITTLE COWBOY KNOW-HOW ON BUSY CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY

"Instead of a citation, the ‘suspect’ made a four-legged getaway and vanished into the East Texas woods," Wallace wrote on Facebook.

"Just another night shift where anything can happen," the sheriff added.

Wallace later assured viewers that the doe was unharmed and "made a full recovery."

The unexpected roadside encounter quickly found an audience online, with Wallace saying the video has been viewed more than 10 million times.

item.title: Bessent predicts oil prices could drop as low as $40 after Iran conflict ends and supply floods market
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could drop to between $40 and $50 after the Iran conflict ends, citing massive supply ready to hit the market.
item.content:encoded:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could fall to between $40 and $50 per barrel once the Iran conflict ends, arguing that abundant supply is poised to hit the market after constraints ease.

Bessent asserted that the American economy is "very strong" and even accelerating, saying that the country is experiencing a "productivity burst" during an interview on "My View with Lara Trump."

"On the other side of this, we actually could see oil prices $40 or $50 because there's so much supply coming on. It's just constricted right now," he told Fox News host Lara Trump.

IRAN WARNS SHIPS OF 'FORCEFUL RESPONSE' AS US-BACKED HORMUZ ROUTE CHALLENGES TEHRAN'S GRIP

"So my message is: Underlying economy is very strong. Job growth is strong. Wage growth is strong."

The "energy supply shock" is only temporary, Bessent said, calling the United States an "energy superpower" and a leader in artificial intelligence and global computing power.

BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME

"Americans, on average, are breaking even. Working-class Americans at the bottom of the wage spectrum are doing a little better than inflation, but we don't believe that that is acceptable," the Treasury chief said.

"But what is the good news is that these wage increases are going to keep going. We've got a manufacturing renaissance, a construction renaissance. So the wages will keep going, this war will end, and those will turn into real wage gains."

LIZ PEEK: THE TRUMP ECONOMY IS DOING BETTER THAN THE MEDIA WANT TO ADMIT

Bessent's comments come as tension between Washington, D.C., and Tehran show no sign of cooling following Saturday’s U.S. strikes on Iranian tankers.

He predicted that the Strait of Hormuz would soon become less crucial to global oil trade as Gulf nations work to construct alternative pipeline routes that will allow them to circumnavigate the tumultuous waters, diminishing Iran's ability to threaten oil flows.

"This is the greatest economic isolation operation in the history of the world. We are going to asphyxiate this regime," Bessent said, adding that the combination of the blockade and sanctions is "one of the most powerful one-two punches in the history of economic isolation."

"I think we are going to get to the other side of this Iran conflict with a safer world, with an Iran that cannot have a nuclear weapon, and that we are in the lift-off phase."

item.title: Terry Bradshaw opens up about mortality after beating cancer twice: 'Am I going to heaven?'
item.description: Terry Bradshaw reveals how two cancer diagnoses reshaped his Christian faith and marriage in a raw podcast interview ahead of his new memoir release.
item.content:encoded:
Pro Football Hall of Famer and longtime FOX NFL Sunday co-host Terry Bradshaw opened up Wednesday on William Shatner and Melanie Shatner Gretsch's "No Time But Now" podcast about confronting his mortality after battling two forms of cancer, explaining how the health scares deepened his Christian faith and changed the way he approaches his marriage, family and remaining years ahead of the release of his new memoir.

"My thoughts were about dying. Am I going to heaven? Am I a good enough man? Have I been a good enough Christian? Have I been kind to people? Am I going to heaven?" Bradshaw said.

Bradshaw's reflections followed two cancer diagnoses that he previously disclosed publicly in 2022. Fox News Digital reported at the time that Bradshaw was diagnosed with bladder cancer in November 2021 and underwent surgery and treatment at Yale University Medical Center. Months later, an MRI prompted by neck pain revealed a Merkel cell tumor, a rare form of skin cancer, in his neck.

DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

Bradshaw recounted on the podcast that he initially kept his first diagnosis private and focused on whether doctors believed it could be treated rather than dwelling on the possibility of dying.

"I didn't feel panic. I didn't think death. My I'm pretty sure I said, ‘Well, curable.’ Yeah. The doctor thinks in 6 weeks," Bradshaw said. "And so I never once went, ‘Oh, I got to get my house in order. I got to do this.’ I just said, ‘Okay, curable.’ That's what I needed to hear."

The second diagnosis came shortly after Bradshaw completed treatment for bladder cancer. He said doctors found Merkel cell cancer in his parotid gland area, leading to surgery that removed 27 lymph nodes followed by six weeks of radiation treatments.

WILLIAM SHATNER AND DAUGHTER MELANIE REVEAL THEY BATTLED STAGE 4 CANCER AT THE SAME TIME

The National Cancer Institute describes Merkel cell carcinoma as a "very rare" skin cancer that tends to grow quickly and can spread at an early stage, frequently beginning on sun-exposed areas including the head and neck.

Bradshaw told Shatner that although he understands cancer could return, his faith helped shape how he views death.

"No, death did not frighten me. It did not in any way frighten me. Now, that's easy to say because I haven't been told you're dying. Well, you're going to die," Bradshaw said.

"I know I'm going to die. And when that time comes, how will I handle that with grace and strength and an understanding that God loves me? I'm going to go to heaven. I'm going to see my family again with it. Yes, that's going to be my, that's going to be my strength," he continued.

JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

The former Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback said surviving cancer also changed how he approaches life with his wife, Tammy, including a desire to travel more and spend their time together differently.

"I want her to have more happiness than she ever thought possible. To me, that just makes that fills my that fills my spirit. That fills me with joy," Bradshaw said.

"To know that, you know, that I'm a good husband now. I'm a good husband now. And I've got a great wife and I want her to know what it's like to really feel loved."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Bradshaw's comments came ahead of the Oct. 13 release of "Looking for Terry: A Memoir," his first memoir in more than two decades. Publisher Harper Select said the book will examine Bradshaw's battle with cancer, depression, faith and the public persona he developed during more than five decades in football and television.

Bradshaw was the No. 1 overall pick in the 1970 NFL Draft and led Pittsburgh to four Super Bowl championships, winning Super Bowl MVP twice before his 1989 induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He remains a co-host of FOX NFL Sunday, with FOX Sports confirming Bradshaw's return for the 2026 NFL season.

item.title: Pro wrestler Andy Williams, who performed as The Butcher, dead at 48
item.description: Andy Williams, known as The Butcher, collapsed after a match at Mr. Smalls Theater in Millvale, Pennsylvania, where doctors administered CPR.
item.content:encoded:
Andy Williams, the pro wrestler known as The Butcher who performed in several promotions including All Elite Wrestling (AEW), died after suffering a medical emergency during a show.

Williams, 48, was in a match with his tag team partner Jesse Guilmette (known as The Blade) at Enjoy Wrestling at Mr. Smalls Theater in Millvale, Pennsylvania, on Friday night. The promotion said Williams collapsed at the end of his match.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

"Our doctors on staff tended to him immediately, administering CPR until the ambulance arrived," the company said. "We sent everyone home and are at the hospital now waiting for more information."

The Allegheny County Medical Examiner's Office told TMZ on Sunday that Williams had died. OutKick Dropkick reached out to authorities for comment.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Williams was also a musician in a band called Every Time I Die.

He started training as a wrestler in the early 2010s and made his debut on the scene in 2015. He and Guilmette began to team up in 2017 and called themselves The Butcher and The Blade. They appeared in several promotions, including AEW, Ring of Honor (ROH), Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) and elsewhere.

The pro wrestling world reacted to word of Williams’ death on social media.

Williams was a guitarist for Every Time I Die from 1998 until the band broke up in 2022.

item.title: 8 everyday things that would quit working without data centers
item.description: Data centers power everything from streaming and gaming to AI chatbots and fraud detection. Here's how they quietly run the apps you use daily.
item.content:encoded:
Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence.

Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they rely on them constantly, often without realizing it.

"Data centers have been around for as long as technology has been around," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center."

As more of the economy moves online, data centers have become far more than a niche piece of the tech industry. They are increasingly essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. is home to roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates.

Here are eight ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day.

From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connected to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds.

The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously.

Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers.

ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes.

Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss.

That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work file — but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware.

Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device.

What feels like a simple Google search is actually a complex exchange between your device and powerful servers processing requests at an enormous scale.

When you order something online, data centers help manage inventory, process payments, make product recommendations and track packages to your door. They also allow retailers to update product availability and pricing quickly as demand changes.

ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI

During major shopping events such as Black Friday, those systems have to handle a surge of shoppers and transactions without crashing.

Google Maps, Waze and other navigation services depend on computing infrastructure to process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time. They combine information from roads, users, businesses and mapping systems to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes.

Without the data centers behind them, navigation apps would not be able to react as quickly to accidents, congestion or changing road conditions.

Video calls, cloud-based software, shared documents and workplace messaging all rely heavily on data-center infrastructure. Every Zoom meeting, Slack message and live edit to a shared file depends on servers that keep information synced between people working from different locations.

THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

For many companies, data centers have become as essential to day-to-day operations as office space, phones and electricity.

Every time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, generates an image or uses an AI-powered search feature, data centers provide the computing power working behind the screen. Those requests require far more processing than a basic web search because the systems must analyze information and generate a response in real time.

That is a major reason the technology industry is racing to build bigger and more powerful data centers, often equipped with specialized chips designed for AI workloads.

GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE

In addition, autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics, scientific research and other emerging technologies require increasingly powerful computing infrastructure. Data centers help train the AI systems behind those tools, process huge volumes of data and support the software that allows them to improve over time.

item.title: Angry locals block famous beach as mass tourism protests escalate at vacation hot spot
item.description: Around 100 residents occupied Cala Saladeta beach in Ibiza to protest tourist overcrowding, demanding that locals reclaim the island's public spaces from visitors.
item.content:encoded:
Some 100 residents staged an occupation of a beach in Ibiza recently to protest overtourism amid growing frustration over mass tourism in Spain — and more action is apparently planned. 

The group gathered at Cala Saladeta, a popular tourist beach, last week, according to Balearic public broadcaster IB3.

The protest was organized by the Ibiza Youth Association, a local youth group.

INFLUENCERS REACHING PEAK BACKLASH AFTER SUMMER OF RUINED DESTINATIONS AND EXPERIENCES FOR AMERICANS 

Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea.

The island is visited by many tourists, with its population swelling during the summer months.

Known to locals as Eivissa, Ibiza received nearly 1.2 million tourists in the second quarter of 2025, according to data from the Balearic Islands Statistics Institute.

Organizers rallied "against tourist overcrowding," IB3 reported, and activists handed out watermelon as part of a demand "that residents be able to enjoy the island's public spaces."

CRUISE SHIP CRACKDOWN HITS TOURIST HOT SPOT AS CITY FAST-TRACKS NEW VISITOR TAX

The group said in its manifesto that "our land and our culture are being directly pushed out of public spaces, and increasingly out of private spaces, as well, displayed solely as tourist attractions," according to local outlet CadeNA SER.

The manifesto also decried a tourism model catering to "wealthy foreigners and famous partygoers," while arguing that housing, food and other living costs have become unaffordable for residents.

"[Young people are] fed up with not being able to enjoy [the island] as tourists do, because we believe we can no longer continue giving up spaces to the visitors brought by this extractive tourism model, which makes our lives in Ibiza more precarious," the manifesto added, per Cadena SER.

The island's coves, which attract tourists during the busy summer season, were also a focus of the group's manifesto.

The coves "should become our coves again, clean and peaceful," the manifesto said.

"We have decided that we want to reclaim places of tranquility, including during the summer," the statement added.

In response to the recent protests, Ibiza Island Council President Vicent Marí said the island has been a "pioneer" in combating tourist overcrowding, according to Cadena SER.

The Ibiza demonstration comes amid broader tensions surrounding mass tourism across Spain.

In recent years, Barcelona residents have taken to the streets to protest mass tourism, with some demonstrators spraying visitors with water guns.

On Mallorca, another of Spain's Balearic Islands, viral videos showed pickpockets targeting tourists near the island's capital of Palma.

item.title: How Charlie Kirk inspired his mentor's fight to defend reality
item.description: Frank Turek stood feet away when Charlie Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University. Now his new book carries on Kirk's apologetics mission.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, author Frank Turek has defended the idea that a Christian worldview offers the truest explanation of reality. The murder of his close friend, Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk one year ago, only reinforced that conviction.

Now, Turek is sharing those beliefs in his new book, "The War on Reality: Recovering Truth in a World that Celebrates Lies," co-authored with Phoenix Hayes. The book argues that popular culture views about the family, gender, education and politics defy logic and aims to equip Christians to challenge these beliefs.

Kirk's wife, Erika, wrote the foreword for the book, in which Turek says she reveals the source of her late husband's quiet confidence during hostile debates on college campuses.

BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME

"She writes that the reason Charlie would go to college campuses and not get flustered is because he knew that the foundation of his belief was true — that there is a God, he is not Him," Turek told Fox News Digital. 

"He has put us on this earth to know him and to make him known through Jesus," Turek said. "And everything else is really just details. And so he could stand firm on a college campus despite any kind of threat or despite any question that might come his way. But he knew he had to be prepared to answer those questions."

As an example of this "war on reality," Turek pointed to the debate over transgender issues, which he argued has caused immeasurable harm to women and children.

"It's a contradictory worldview that tragically is hurting children the most, because we have people now, politicians and mostly Democrats saying... what we ought to do is transition children that are confused about their sexuality," Turek said. "This is not care, this is child abuse. It's a war on women, by the way, because now women aren't protected in women's sports or in women's changing facilities."

Turek mentored Kirk on applying strategies he discusses in the book, such as employing the laws of logic and identifying fallacies when responding to polarizing cultural topics. 

Their friendship began in 2020 after Kirk asked Turek to mentor him in Christian apologetics, which is the practice of defending Christianity with evidence and reasoning. Turek said their bond deepened over time until he came to view Kirk as a son.

BILL MAHER TO APPEAR IN CHARLIE KIRK DOCUMENTARY, REMEMBERS LOVING HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE TPUSA LEADER

"Charlie was the same person offstage that he was onstage. He was somebody that was always trying to learn," Turek told Fox News Digital. "It can be hard to mentor somebody smarter than you, but not with Charlie, because the only thing that exceeded his intellect was his humility. The few things that I knew that he wanted to know, he asked me to tell him. So we would get together and discuss questions he might get on a college campus, because I've been presenting on college campuses for about 20 years. And we would sharpen one another."

Turek was standing just feet away when Kirk was shot and killed Sept. 10 at Utah Valley University during the first stop of TPUSA’s "The American Comeback Tour."

At Kirk's memorial service weeks later, Turek reflected on his friend's faith.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Now, I want you to know that Charlie, right now, is in heaven," Turek said at the service. "Not because he was a great husband and father, not because he saved millions of kids out of darkness on college campuses, not because he changed minds and chased votes to save the country, not because he sacrificed himself for his Savior. Charlie Kirk is in heaven because his Savior sacrificed himself for Charlie Kirk."

Ultimately, Turek hopes his book encourages Christians and churches to speak out boldly in the public square and to carry on Kirk's legacy.

"I hear from pastors all the time, 'I don't get involved in politics, I just preach the gospel,' to which I say to them, 'I guess you don't think the gospel is very important then.' And they say, 'Well, what do you mean?' And I say, 'Because the laws that are made politically can affect your ability to preach and live the gospel'... So for no other reason, Christians have to be involved in politics to protect our ability to preach and live the gospel, to have religious freedom," Turek said. 

"The second reason, major reason, is because we're called to love one another. And God set up governments to protect innocent people from evil. According to Romans 13, the government is supposed to punish wrongdoers. Why will we not put laws in place as Christians to punish people who are doing evil. We should," Turek said.

item.title: Mysterious settlement discovered after residents seemingly packed up and vanished
item.description: A medieval village near Halberstadt in Saxony-Anhalt was abandoned in a "highly orderly fashion," archaeologists say — but why the residents left remains a mystery.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists recently uncovered the remains of a medieval village that was mysteriously abandoned in Germany — raising questions about why its residents packed up and left.

The excavation at the Am Frevelgraben site in Halberstadt, in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, revealed numerous traces of a medieval settlement, including parts of a multi-tiered ditch system.

The State Office for Monument Preservation and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt announced the findings on Aug. 24.

UNEXPECTED ANCIENT COMPLEX EMERGES NEAR BIBLICAL CITY LINKED TO JONAH AND ST PETER

Archaeologists began excavating the site in March ahead of the development of a nearby industrial park, officials said. 

Historical maps suggest the settlement may be the remains of a medieval village known as Kühlingen.

Archaeologists documented rows of pit houses, settlement pits and two wells at the site, while other traces suggest residents also made extensive use of the nearby riverbank.

Overlapping features and houses built directly next to one another indicate the settlement developed in two phases, officials said — with its footprint shifting as new homes were constructed.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT

Despite the well-preserved remains, however, archaeologists found surprisingly few artifacts — a detail officials found remarkable.

"A few scattered ceramic shards and a handful of metal finds, including, for example, a bronze tap, fittings, and belt buckets, certainly represent only a fraction of the former possessions of the inhabitants," the release said.

The settlement was abandoned "in a highly orderly fashion," Oliver Dietrich, a spokesperson for the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, told Fox News Digital.

"It was indeed striking how few artifacts were left behind," he said. "Medieval deserted villages typically yield a wealth of artifacts."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Dietrich said archaeologists found no evidence of destruction or fire at the site, and said the reason behind the abandonment "remains a mystery at this time."

"Further analysis will produce further insights into the abandonment process," he said.

The settlement is "clearly medieval," though researchers are not sure precisely when it was abandoned, Dietrich added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Because of the scarcity of finds, radiocarbon analyses of selected animal bones are expected to provide a precise date," he said.

As fascinating as it is, the expert added that Am Frevelgraben is one of hundreds of deserted medieval villages in Germany.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The most drastic period of abandonment was during the 14th and 15th centuries," Dietrich said, citing the Black Death, migration and climate change.

Often these villages "had too few resources to sustain the people," he said.

The find follows a similar discovery made recently in neighboring Poland.

Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered another abandoned medieval settlement, Stolzenberg, which had remained hidden in a remote forest for centuries.

item.title: Letitia James’ Times Square shooting probe draws GOP criticism over New York’s mental health crisis
item.description: Saritha Komatireddy proposes a new Office of Civil Commitment after the Times Square fatal stabbing, saying New York fails mentally ill people.
item.content:encoded:
New York Attorney General Letitia James is facing scrutiny after opening up a legally required investigation into the police shooting of a woman who fatally stabbed Erin Piacenti, Bank of America executive and a new mother in her first week back to work from maternity leave, in Times Square.

James' office announced on Wednesday that it will be investigating Pamela Cisneros' death, who was wielding two large knives in each hand when officers confronted her following the fatal stabbing. She was ordered to drop the weapons but did not comply and was shot when she moved toward the officers.

Under state law, the Attorney General's Office of Special Investigation is mandated to investigate all deaths that were caused by police officers. However, Republican attorney general candidate Saritha Komatireddy is pushing the Attorney General's Office to take more concrete steps to ensure that another tragic killing or attack caused by a mentally unstable person doesn't happen again. She argued that an investigation into police conduct fails to address the real problem.

"The problem is that we have people who are known dangerous individuals, people with documented mental illness," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "They've been in the courts before, or they've been to the hospitals before. The police know exactly who they are, but we have no ability to take care of them."

REPUBLICANS GET 'AGGRESSIVE' IN FIGHT TO WIN TOP COP SPOTS IN BATTLEGROUND STATES

A campaign spokesperson for James accused Komatireddy of seeking to "score cheap political points off of a tragedy."

"Saritha Komatireddy wants to be Attorney General but doesn’t understand the law," a spokesperson said in an email to Fox News Digital. "Under New York’s Executive Law, the Office of the Attorney General’s Office of Special Investigation is required to investigate any incident where a police officer’s actions may have caused a death, including this one."

However, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has a history of anti-police rhetoric, applauded the officers who stopped Cisneros.

"I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse," Mamdani said at a news conference.

PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION'

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch shared that while Cisneros, who lived in Queens, didn't have an arrest record in the city, there were two times police responded to calls concerning her suffering a mental health crisis.

In March 2019, Cisneros attempted suicide by jumping onto the tracks of the E train and was removed and later hospitalized. In March 2018, police found her in Midtown, where she was screaming, acting belligerent and intoxicated.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Under the state's Mental Hygiene Law, police and doctors can take a person to the hospital for a psychological hold if they are deemed to be a risk to themselves or others, or they can not meet their basic needs — but often times those with severe mental illnesses are released by the hospital back onto the streets hours after being brought in.

LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS

"I was there in Times Square — just a couple of days after this fatal stabbing — and I was walking around and saw severely mentally ill people on the street," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "It's still happening every day, and we need someone who's actually going to propose a real solution and way forward."

TRUMP WANTS TO HELP 146,000 MENTALLY ILL WHO ARE HOMELESS. DEMOCRATS WANT TO STOP HIM

The New York State Office of Mental Health is tasked with overseeing the state's mental health system, which includes 23 psychiatric centers and 6,500 programs overseen by local governments and nonprofits. In addition, Komatireddy said that, if elected, she'd create a new office known as the Office of Civil Commitment that would target and keep tabs on people who are at most risk.

"The Office of Civil Commitment that I'm going to launch will be staffed with both law enforcement personnel and also physicians, and you need both because, under state law, the law requires that physicians certify that someone has the mental state required for involuntary civil commitment," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "So there's nothing like that right now in New York state. There's no office that has both law enforcement and physicians who can work together to get these people off the streets."

Greene County Sheriff Peter Kusminsky told Fox News Digital that his deputies are not trained to handle psychiatric crises — and that the county has nowhere to send people who need real care. Deputies are constantly pulled off patrol for mental-health calls, he said, then left to put those in crisis in hotels because there aren't enough hospital beds available.

"Additionally, we really struggle when we have people in custody who we aren't equipped to handle, and secure beds are even harder to find," Kusminsky said. "It sometimes takes weeks or months to locate once and when we do, they are maybe on the other side of the state and at an exorbitant cost."

"Hotels and motels don’t have doctors, don’t have medicine, don’t have therapy," Komatireddy said. "The state needs to step in."

item.title: WWE Sunday Night's Main Event match card, predictions and more
item.description: Sunday Night's Main Event features Cody Rhodes vs. Randy Orton in a grudge match after a WrestleMania 42 punt left Rhodes' eye swollen shut.
item.content:encoded:
For at least one night, WWE’s Saturday Night’s Main Event will transform into Sunday Night’s Main Event as the showcase will take place in Atlanta on Labor Day weekend.

There are only four matches on the card, but each comes with heightened stakes.

Sunday Night’s Main Event is also set to feature a live performance from hip-hop artist Quavo, who will debut an unreleased track from his forthcoming album "QROMELIFE."

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

Read below for the match card and predictions on what will happen at the State Farm Arena on Sunday night. The event begins at 8 p.m. ET and can be seen on Peacock.

==

A six-woman tag team match will take place to add to the longstanding feud among Charlotte Flair, Alexa Bliss and Tatum Paxley and Jade Cargill, Michin and B-Fab. It feels as though these women have been battling for months. Paxley was added to the fray when she made her SmackDown debut to back up Flair and Bliss. But Cargill, Michin and B-Fab have continuously been scrapping with Flair, Bliss and Paxley with Cargill and Flair seemingly fighting for the top contender spot to Chelsea Green’s women’s title.

Prediction: Flair, Bliss and Paxley put away Cargill, Michin and B-Fab.

==

Baron Corbin returned to WWE and made an immediate impact. He earned a United States Championship shot at SummerSlam and defeated Trick Williams to win the title. Williams has been clawing his way back to the top, eyeing a title return. But he hasn’t been the only who has messed with Corbin. Lil Yachty, Williams’ valet, has kept nipping at Corbin’s heels. He’ll have a chance to help Williams in his match against Corbin. If Lil Yachty lasts at least five minutes in the ring with Corbin, Williams will get a rematch for the U.S. title. Expect some kind of shenanigans to take place in this match.

Prediction: Lil Yachty holds out for as long as he can against Corbin

==

It’s the long-awaited grudge match between WWE superstars Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton. Rhodes owes Orton another lick after getting punted in the head following their WrestleMania 42 Night 1 main event brawl. Rhodes won that match to retain the Undisputed WWE Championship. Orton got the last word with the kick that left Rhodes’ eye swollen. Since Orton’s return, the two have brawled constantly. Rhodes even went for a kill shot at one point. It caused SmackDown GM Nick Aldis to tell them if they continued to fight each other, they would never get a shot at a WWE championship again. It led to some harsh words from Orton, trying to coax Rhodes into hitting him. It didn’t work, but you could feel the tension between the two men building. This match will turn into a good ol’ fashioned slobber knocker.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Prediction: Cody Rhodes comes out on top in this one.

==

There’s no tangible title on the line in this one – there’s only perception. Who is the future of WWE? Bron Breakker has been inside his own head for weeks as he grappled with Oba Femi’s rise in WWE. Breakker was on the mend as Femi defeated Brock Lesnar at WrestleMania 42, won the King of the Ring Tournament and seemingly ended Lesnar’s career at SummerSlam. Breakker failed to dispatch Seth Rollins and only became a tag team champion after Logan Paul got hurt. Breakker has shown that he still has that dog in him but Femi’s rule over the Raw roster has been cataclysmic for his opponents. Both men could very well be champions in the future, but for now, they fight to be the face of what is to come down the road.

Prediction: Breakker needs a win here to go back to the days in which he was considered the man with the loudest bark and the biggest bite. Breakker wins in what might be an upset.

item.title: Livvy Dunne and Brooks Nader join Lane's first Tiger Walk, Tricia Whitaker wants Indiana repeat & tons of meat
item.description: Lane Kiffin's LSU era opened with a dominant 51-10 demolition of Clemson, with Livvy Dunne, Brooks Nader, and Theo Von joining his Tiger Walk.
item.content:encoded:
What a start to the Lane Kiffin era at LSU. After a week of drama surrounding a couple of players who couldn’t make an NFL roster, the Tigers steamrolled Clemson at home without those players on their roster.

It had it all. A rain delay, an awesome halftime interview, and Lane's first Tiger Walk had to have Screencaps in mind. He was accompanied by Livvy Dunne, Brooks Nader, and Theo Von as he confidently strolled to Saturday's game.

Nader, a Louisiana native, set the tone for the entire day. She was part of the festivities in the morning, and it was clear from that moment on that Clemson didn't stand a chance.

SEC LAWYERS, LANE KIFFIN AND DEATH VALLEY: COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S WEEK 1 IS SET FOR FIREWORKS

She wasn’t there to play around. This was a business trip.

Later in the day came Lane's Tiger Walk and his entourage of Louisiana royalty. Nader returned, having made an outfit change, alongside LSU legend and Nader's "Baywatch" co-star and fellow SI Swimsuit model Livvy Dunne.

A LIST OF THE BEST COLLEGE GAMEDAY SIGNS AT LSU DURING SHOW'S 500TH EPISODE

Why was Theo Von there? Well, he's not, as far as I know, making an appearance in either "Baywatch" or SI Swimsuit, but he is a Louisiana native and evidently a friend of Kiffin's.

With an entrance like that, you had better win convincingly. We're talking 50-plus in a one-sided game where Clemson fans were at home tapping out. A 51-10 beat down works.

Something tells me they're going to have a lot of fun in Baton Rouge this season.

Now to another team who allowed points to be scored on them in Week 1. I get it not every team can dominate at home to open the season and manhandle a lesser opponent without allowing them to score a single point like Penn State did.

Some teams need a second to appear on a clock out of thin air. Teams like No. 16 Michigan who struggled and lost the game to Western Michigan until a second that had already ticked off the game clock returned from the dead.

After that miracle, the Wolverines won the game (asterisk) on a second Hail Mary attempt after the first was thrown out of the back of the end zone and showed the game clock at zero before anyone touched the ball.

Western Michigan was robbed. As sad of a game as it was for Michigan, fans storming the field after such an atrocious performance tells you exactly where they are as a football program.

This might count as a win in the record books, but this is a loss to everyone else.

item.title: My father taught me the dignity of labor: We ‘get to’ live, work and love
item.description: After her father’s death, Asra Nomani revisits the quiet acts of service that shaped her life and finally understands the true meaning of the dignity of labor.
item.content:encoded:
My father froze when he saw his professor washing cars.

It was 1962, and Zafar Nomani was a visiting teacher at Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kan., newly arrived from India on a fellowship. One day, riding past a church car wash, he spotted his professor among the people scrubbing down cars beside his students.

For the rest of his life, my father treasured that moment.

"I saw the dignity of labor," he would tell us.

More than six decades later, on this Labor Day weekend, my family is mourning my father, who died in early August at the age of 93 in our adopted hometown of Morgantown, W.Va. And as I negotiate new relationships with his power washer, his weed trimmer, his tools and the daily chores that he quietly managed, pushing a cart at our local Kroger on Patterson Avenue, I find myself reliving – and rewriting – the story of my life with him.

For most of my life, I thought I was challenging the patriarchy. Now I realize I grew and became the investigative journalist that I am because of the patriarch in my life.

I arrived in America from India in the summer of 1969 as a 4-year-old girl and I grew up in the 1970s with feminism, women’s rights and Gloria Steinem, who died this week at 92, just a year younger than my father. I learned to interrogate male power, religious authority and the restrictions that societies imposed on women.

I still believe in the work of empowering women and girls.

But in my father's absence, I have come to understand something I failed to fully appreciate while he was alive: the quiet and largely invisible power of a good patriarch.

I spent much of my life believing my strength came from resisting my father’s authority; after his death, as I grieve his absence from this world, I recognize that much of my strength, intellect and purpose came from the invisible labor he performed to make my independence possible.

I thought I was overcoming the patriarch; I now see that – with his devoted and beloved wife beside him – my father was performing the quiet service that allowed me to become the woman capable of challenging him.

That epiphany has also changed the meaning of "labor" for me.

Labor, I now understand, isn't just the work we perform from 9 to 5, as Dolly Parton, another national treasure lost this summer, sang. Some of the most important labor of our lives is never entered on a time sheet. It is the ordinary caregiving through which people provide one another shelter, safety, security.

This summer, for two months, I helped care for my father with my family in hospital rooms at our local hospital. His last breath came in Room 8.

Amid the oxygen tubes, medications, alarms and fear, I fell in love with my father all over again. I resurrected the spirit of the girl who once lay against his belly listening to stories about the kings and queens of India. I remembered the girl who arrived in the U.S. At the time, my father was a Ph.D. student and our family lived in poverty in graduate-student housing in Piscataway, N.J., in a humble red two-bedroom home converted from military barracks on Bevier Road. In the winters, my parents turned on the oven to heat the home. But my parents still found a way to throw me a birthday party in our backyard.

The grievances and misunderstandings that accumulated over a lifetime fell away.

What remained was the gratitude my father had modeled for me through the way he lived his life.

His philosophy was not "I have to," but "I get to."

My father never lived from the premise that life had victimized him. He didn't organize his days around the complaints of "I have to..." I have to work. I have to study. I have to take care of my family.

His philosophy was exactly the opposite: the gratitude of "I get to..." I get to. I get to work. I get to study. I get to take care of my family.

That philosophy had been forged long ago in his response to adversity and suffering.

JASON MIYARES: MOTHER FLED CUBA AND FOUND THE FREEDOM TOO MANY AMERICANS NOW FORGET

Born in the summer of 1933 in India under British colonial rule, my father survived the Bengal famine of 1943 when the British diverted food from India to military troops fighting in World War II. As a boy in Hyderabad, India, he stood in lines for food aid from the United States. Tears came to his eyes decades later when he remembered the coarse red sorghum scraping his throat as he swallowed grain he said had been intended as animal feed.

But the lesson he took from hunger wasn't "Look what I suffered."

It was "I get to eat."

After being wed to my mother in 1962 in an arranged marriage, he confided in her on their wedding night his philosophy of transcending suffering with a simple purpose: "Serve humanity." That led him to the car wash moment in Kansas.

Years later, while studying at Rutgers University, my mother babysat other people's children to help raise enough money for airfare for my brother, Mustafa, and me to reunite with our parents.

When we moved to Morgantown, W.Va., in 1975, and he began building his career as a professor of nutrition, he worked from morning until night. He didn't begrudge those hours.

Instead, his ethos was plainly simple: "I get to work."

He rarely announced this philosophy. Like many men of his generation, he wasn't fluent in the modern language of feelings.

His love language was service.

And what that service meant for me, especially as a girl growing up in the 1970s, was remarkable.

A stricter interpretation of Islam was spreading around the world, fueled in part by the religious forces rising from Saudi Arabia and the new Islamic Republic of Iran. Once, my father was told that I needed to cover my legs because otherwise they were haram, or Islamically forbidden.

My father didn't stop me from running track. He was a girl dad before it was a thing.

One cold, rainy day in the spring of 1978, after I had run a mile race on the track at the West Virginia University Coliseum, I stood weeping at the finish line because my hands were so painfully frozen. My father swooped down from the bleachers, took my hands inside his and breathed his hot breath over them, again and again, thawing my fingers.

He didn't complain about the rain. He didn't complain about standing there in the cold. His actions said: "I get to care for my daughter."

DANA PERINO: FIVE IMPORTANT LESSONS FROM MY FATHER FOR EVERY PROUD GIRL DAD

My father’s labor of love often happened behind the wheel, driving us everywhere — to school, to opportunities, to airports, to the next place where one of us might grow.

In the summer of 1981, my father drove me to Pittsburgh International Airport for a National Science Foundation camp in Tahlequah, Okla. While I was away, he turned his attention to another journey: helping my mother, Sajida, realize her dream of becoming the first woman in her family to start a business. He stayed up through the night, hand-drawing the window sign for her boutique, Ain’s International, named using the last part of my middle name. Then he drove around town, stapling promotional flyers for her store on bulletin boards around campus.

He saw dignity in every act of service: "I get to help my wife."

She built a store on High Street in downtown Morgantown that became a home away from home for generations of college students. They sat on stools at her counter and told her their stories, their heartbreaks and their troubles.

As a first-generation immigrant, my father understood that opportunity wasn't something to hoard. It was something to create for others.

When I decided to become a journalist, my father knew well the expectations of our culture: a daughter eventually left her father's home for her husband's.

But when I wanted an internship in New York City in the summer of 1983, he got into our Subaru and drove me from our home on Cottonwood Street to an interview at Harper's Magazine on Park Avenue.

Years later, in Room 8, he still remembered one of the details of that trip. After dropping me off, he drove to New Jersey because the parking was cheaper. He had never complained to me about the cost of parking. He reveled in the act of service: "I get to drive my daughter toward an opportunity."

When I went to graduate school in Washington, D.C., in the late summer of 1986, he climbed back behind the wheel of our Subaru and drove with me again, helping me hunt for an apartment on Massachusetts Avenue and Embassy Row for a rent of $300 a month that my mother and he paid.

His work was sacred: "I get to help my daughter build her life."

But growing up inside that shelter didn't mean I always recognized it.

When I was in my late 20s, a successful reporter at the Wall Street Journal's Washington, D.C., bureau, I went to a psychologist carrying the grievances young adults can accumulate against their parents. I catalogued what my father had done wrong, leaving my brother and me in India with his parents while he settled with my mother in the U.S., leaving me with "abandonment issues." I even persuaded my father to come into a therapy session on Wisconsin Avenue NW and listen as I poured out my anger.

He could have dismissed me. He could have invoked his authority. He could have walked out. Instead, he listened.

I even complained that he hadn't made me a baby book as American children enjoyed. He didn't grouse. He filled out a baby book for me with hand-drawn pictures.

Again, when confronted with my pain, his instinct wasn't to defend himself. It was to do something.

MARK MERRILL: THE FOUNDING FATHERS GAVE US AMERICA. 250 YEARS LATER, WE STILL DEPEND ON GOOD DADS

When I went to Pakistan after the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, to report on extremism, I couldn't have imagined what awaited me. Then my friend and colleague from the Wall Street Journal, Daniel Pearl, was kidnapped after he left a home I had rented in Karachi.

I called home. My father told me, "It is your farz," or duty, "to help your friend."

That was another definition of my father's sense of labor. Duty wasn't drudgery. Duty was love and friendship expressed through action.

Then, in one of the darkest periods of my life, I saw my father's sense of sacred duty express itself for me.

Weeks later, I learned I was pregnant. I had fallen in love with a boyfriend in Karachi, and we had talked about marriage. But amid the dragnet of intelligence and military officials surrounding my house as they searched for Danny, he disappeared, frightened by what was unfolding around us.

I broke the news to my mother, afraid of how my father would react. In Pakistan, it's a crime to be unmarried and pregnant.

Then my father sent me an email with just three words: "I love you."

There was no lecture. No shame. His message, as I now understand it, was a divine gift: You get to be a mother.

And, characteristically, he turned those words into work.

Over the next months, my father finished a new bedroom in his home for my baby and me. When he picked me up at the airport, his fingernails were coated with the baby-blue paint that is still on those walls.

Later, when I raised my son as a single mother, my father retired and quietly stepped into another job with a clear mission: Helping care for his grandson, reading the morning newspaper with my boy on his lap. During the challenging middle-school years, he moved in with us, sleeping on the lower bunk of my son's bunkbed and cooking us biryani lamb-and-rice dishes for dinner with packets of Shan Foods boxed spices.

Even the most mundane crises became occasions for service — and, inevitably, for science.

When a tree fell in our yard, he put my son's bicycle helmet on his own head as a homemade safety helmet and went outside to study the problem. He examined the angles, the weight, the branches and the physics. He approached the challenge with the same zest he tackled every adversity: "I get to clear the tree."

When I interviewed him about his strategy, he articulated the scientific method he had instilled in me: "Life is multivariate."

As a scientist, my father studied the Islamic practice of fasting from sunup to sundown during the month of Ramadan and became a pioneer in research that would later help inform what we now understand as intermittent fasting.

But the most important experiment he conducted, at least for me, was an experiment in unconditional love. Ours was a family that was an experiment in assimilation, integration and authenticity.

Once I asked him why he hadn't shamed me when I returned home pregnant without a wedding ring.

Life was an experiment, he told me. Learn from everything.

That was how I learned to become a researcher, an investigator and a journalist. He taught me to look at evidence, revise conclusions and challenge assumptions, even when they are our own.

Most remarkably, he was willing to apply that scientific openness to himself.

When I went to our mosque in Morgantown in the fall of 2003 and an elder told me, "Sister, take the back door," my father stood with me and supported me when I walked in through the front door. As a board member of the mosque, he wept in the kitchen, pleading with the other board members, "Make room for our daughters."

Mosque leaders didn't agree with him. Eventually, he surrendered his authority and stepped down from the board.

At home, he and I often debated gender dynamics and global politics in our kitchen.

I argued with him fiercely. I challenged him. And, each time, he allowed himself to be challenged by his daughter. And he kept supporting me, one cold morning standing with me and other women at the intersection of Johnnycake Road and Adamsview Road in Windsor Mill, Md., holding a sign we'd printed at Kinko's in the pre-dawn morning, advocating for "#MuslimReform" and women's rights.

When I faced online death threats and character assassination, my father invented a moniker, "Zaf4Peace," to defend his daughter on comment boards.

For years, I thought my strength came from pushing against him. Now I understand that my strength came because of his courage in giving me room to push.

An immigrant father in a new culture, so foreign from his own, he grew with me, and, in that shelter, I was able to grow.

That recognition makes the ordinary moments feel more poignant now.

He wasn’t perfect. Neither was I. And I carry many regrets for decades I wish I could relive from a place of gratitude for the father who was actually in front of me, rather than for some Hallmark version of the patriarchy imagined.

I have understood in my father’s absence that we were on a lifelong journey together. In 2011, when I got a seat on a flight to Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, to cover the military tribunal of the man who confessed to murdering my friend Danny and to orchestrating the Sept. 11 attacks, I could have taken a taxi to Andrews Air Force Base. Instead, I asked my father to drive me. And I got cranky when he braked at green lights.

How irrelevant that annoyance suddenly seems. How precious the ride feels now.

Years later, when I was struggling through heartbreak, a psychologist introduced me to positive psychology and told me, "Plant flowers; don’t feed the wolf."

I repeated the words to my father.

He went to Home Depot, came back with potted rose bushes and planted them for me. Then he listened quietly as I wept beside him. He didn't have words for me, just quiet labor.

Looking back, I see that pattern everywhere.

DAVID MARCUS: LABOR DAY IS FOR THE PROUD WORKERS WHO BUILT OUR COUNTRY

Love expressed itself in our lives through labor. The labor of warming your daughter's frozen hands. The labor of tending to a fallen tree. The labor of changing your mind. The labor of planting flowers.

The labor of defending your daughter's right to walk through the front door. The labor of getting up every morning and looking around at the people entrusted to your care and not thinking, I have to take medicine, but: I get to. Even in sickness, my father lived in gratitude, whispering, "Thank you," through the respiratory treatments that marked his last days.

This summer, the man who had spent a lifetime caring for us became the one who needed care. In doing so, he gave us the precious gift of being able to serve him. At his bedside was the next generation he loved – Safiyyah, Samir, Shibli and Kenzy – whispering their adoration softly into his ear.

And then came the final reversal. This summer, in Room 8, my father became the one whose hands grew cold.

Nearly five decades after that rainy track meet, I sat beside him in Room 8 and held those hands that had once enclosed mine. His muscles were tired. His body was failing. I held his hands, and I breathed my warm air onto his fingers, just as he had once breathed onto mine.

This summer, I was able to say again and again: "I get to care for my father." His lesson of unconditional love and service had come full circle.

Even after his last breath, he had one more lesson to teach me about love.

When it came time for my father's funeral prayer, I didn't demand to walk through the mosque's front door.

I stood sentry outside.

There was a time when I might have understood that moment principally as a confrontation with patriarchy.

I understood it differently now. I was there with my father.

For one day, the argument was no longer important. Honoring him was.

The professor whom my father saw washing cars in Kansas in 1962 couldn't have ever known what the young scholar from India would carry away from that encounter.

My father called it the dignity of labor.

It took me a lifetime to understand how completely my father embodied that value.

And it took his passing from this Earth for me to recognize how completely he had taught it to me.

The dignity of labor isn't simply the dignity of a paycheck, a profession or physical work.

It is the dignity in serving another human being without humiliation or reward. It is the dignity in making another person's life possible. It is the dignity of doing the work nobody applauds.

It is the dignity of a father standing in the rain, warming his daughter's hands.

And this Labor Day, with my father's weed trimmer and power washer waiting for me, I feel his presence everywhere amid his absence. I finally understand the inheritance he left behind.

There is work to do, serving our families and this world.

And we get to do it.

item.title: Sydney Sweeney, Scooter Braun romance faces biggest challenge yet as expert warns couple to 'be prepared'
item.description: A year after first meeting at Jeff Bezos' wedding in Venice, Sydney Sweeney and Scooter Braun hit a major new milestone involving his children.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney Sweeney and Scooter Braun's relationship reached a new milestone one year after the pair first met.

The power couple was recently spotted on a casual smoothie date with his two children in Los Angeles, Calif., according to images obtained by TMZ.

While Sweeney, 28, and Braun, 45, have remained private about their budding romance, experts warned that the couple needs to "be prepared" now that kids are part of the relationship.

SYDNEY SWEENEY, SCOOTER BRAUN PACK ON PDA DURING ROMANTIC GONDOLA RIDE IN VENICE

Licensed clinical psychotherapist Robin Hamilton emphasized the importance of treating "the kids as if they are individuals who didn't choose to be celebrities."

"You want to keep their personal lives personal and their parents' celebrity lives theirs," Hamilton told Fox News Digital. Just keep it separate because people are going to be approaching these kids. They're going to ask them questions... So they have to be prepared.

"Prepare the kids to navigate those questions and how people are going to approach them if they want them to be in the public life. I would say like being deliberate about spending quality time where there's nobody commenting on you, there are no cameras there and just, you know, not putting all that pressure on the kids right now, because it's a lot."

SYDNEY SWEENEY SIZZLES IN WONDER WOMAN CORSET COSTUME AS SHE SOAKS UP SUMMER ROMANCE WITH SCOOTER BRAUN

She added, "We see what happens to people who are child stars when they grow up. Sometimes they can't handle all of that stuff."

Braun and Sweeney first sparked romance rumors in June 2025 at Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos' wedding in Venice, Italy.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Originally it was reported the two were "casually" hooking up, but by December, insiders hinted the relationship was more serious.

"Scooter and Sydney are going strong and things between them are great," a source told People at the time. "They're in a committed relationship and things are serious."

Braun was Sweeney's date for the April premiere of "Euphoria" season three, and she hard-launched their romance in May after sharing a photo on social media with him at the premiere.

Nicole Moore, communications and relationship expert, explained how Sweeney and Braun work well together because they "appear to be prioritizing quality time together over posing for the cameras."

"Most celebrity romances have a short expiration date, so the fact that Sydney Sweeney and Scooter Braun have reached the stage of Sydney being involved with his kids is significant," Moore told Fox News Digital.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Many parents don’t introduce a love interest to their children unless they’re confident the connection will be a lasting one, so it’s possible that Scooter sees Sydney as a long-term mate."

Braun was married to entrepreneur and activist Yael Cohen from 2014 until their divorce was finalized in 2022, and they share three children.

Sweeney's relationship with the mega-manager appeared to be stronger than ever, but Moore warned that dynamics may shift if she's "expected to take on a parental figure role."
